text: I see you are experiencing shortness of breath, increased abdominal girth, and a large ovarian mass. Have you noticed any recent unintentional weight loss or changes in your bowel or bladder habits?

speaker: Patient
text: 40-year-old nulliparous woman. The patient reports experiencing shortness of breath and noticeable increase in abdominal size over the past month. She denies any significant medical history, previous surgeries, or use of medications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any abdominal pain, bloating, or early satiety, and have you noticed any vaginal bleeding or discharge? Are you currently pregnant?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Shortness of breath. I also have Increased abdominal girth, Fatigue, No significant weight loss or gain.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Pelvic_Ultrasound: Large mass in the right ovary, significant ascites present. CA-125: Normal.

speaker: Doctor
text: The presence of ascites and a large ovarian mass with shortness of breath, despite a normal CA-125, is highly suggestive of Meigs syndrome. I will request imaging to check for pleural effusion, which is a key diagnostic criterion. REQUEST IMAGES

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant medical history. Social history: Non-smoker, does not consume alcohol regularly. Works as a high school teacher.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any chest pain or discomfort when breathing deeply, and has the shortness of breath worsened when lying flat? I need to confirm if there is a right-sided pleural effusion, which would complete the classic triad for Meigs syndrome.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies fever, night sweats, chest pain, or swelling in the legs. She has not noticed any changes in bowel or urinary habits.

speaker: Doctor
text: The clinical triad of an ovarian mass, ascites, and pleural effusion with a normal CA-125 strongly points to Meigs syndrome. DIAGNOSIS READY: Meigs syndrome
